title: How Explicit Teaching Became Over-Scripted
author: Trudy Mayo
summary: Trudy Mayo observes that many teachers are exhausted not by teaching but by the preparation demanded by explicit instruction: scripting every sentence, worked example and student response. She argues that structure and scripting have become confused, and that polished slide decks and click-through examples have turned lessons into performances rather than responsive instruction. Her position is that slides are valuable for routines, transitions and reducing cognitive load, but become a problem when they replace the teaching rather than support it. Worked examples should be modelled live with teacher thinking aloud, and guided practice should involve active thinking rather than silent copying. The remedy is to plan the structure, not script the performance, so that teachers have room to read the room and reteach in the moment. The post closes with a promotion for the author's paid portal.
points: Mayo distinguishes structure, which makes lessons predictable and lowers load, from scripting, which exhausts teachers and crowds out responsiveness.
Slides become a problem when they are the teaching rather than a support for it.
Worked examples should be modelled live through thinking aloud and questioning, not revealed slide by slide to passive watchers.
Social media and school demands for consistency have normalised polished lesson design that looks like effective teaching from the outside.
quotes: Because at its core, explicit teaching is actually meant to reduce cognitive load for both students and teachers through clarity, consistency and carefully sequenced instruction. The irony is that many teachers now feel more cognitively overloaded than ever trying to implement it.
I think part of the reason is that structure and scripting have slowly become confused with each other. They are not the same thing.
The issue is not the existence of slides. The issue is when the slides become the teaching itself instead of supporting the teaching.
Some of the strongest explicit teaching classrooms I have observed were never rigid or robotic. The teacher was constantly reading the room.
A worked example should not just be revealed slide by slide while students passively watch. It should be modelled live through teacher thinking aloud, questioning and decision-making.
Guided practice should not become silent copying from the board. It should involve active thinking, participation and responsive support while misconceptions are identified and addressed.
One of the biggest shifts for me over the years was realising that I did not need to script the performance of teaching. I needed to plan the structure. That distinction changed everything.
